prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Two floors up, at the corner of Hearst and Shattuck, he’s clamped for good in an iron lung. When it’s time to eat he nudges his head a sweaty mile to the edge of the pillow. It takes a while. His brilliant bloodshot light-blue eyes steer me from cupboard to fridge: he would like his chicken burrito cut into bite-size pieces, a bent straw for his glass of water, please. How does the body live its only life in a cage? I watch him compute the distance from bar to bar, and squeeze between them with a violent compression, a fury of bursting free that doesn’t last. His will is a crowbar, angled to pry up the rooted intractable weight of matter. I watch him slyly, I check out the way he does it. He does it. But pain in its absolute privacy weighs what it weighs. I come here to study the soul, posing one question a dozen ways, most of them silent. “If I’m only a body,” he laughs, “I’m up shit creek.” His laugh a gritty eruption of rock, salt and breath. Like me he writes poems but he does it letter by letter on a propped keyboard, the mouth-stick wobbling between his teeth. That kind of speed keeps a poet accountable. He won’t ever say, “The grass is very green” when it’s only green.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Two, Hearst, Shattuck

outputs.L1:
Two floors up, at the corner of Hearst and Shattuck, he is permanently confined to an iron lung. When it is time to eat, he inches his head a sweaty mile to the edge of the pillow. It takes a while. His brilliant, bloodshot, light-blue eyes guide me from cupboard to refrigerator: he would like his chicken burrito cut into bite-size pieces and a bent straw for his glass of water, please.

How does the body live its only life in a cage? I watch him calculate the distance from bar to bar and squeeze between them with a violent compression, a fury of bursting free that does not last. His will is a crowbar, angled to pry up the rooted, intractable weight of matter. I watch him slyly; I study the way he does it. He does it. But pain, in its absolute privacy, weighs what it weighs.

I come here to study the soul, posing one question a dozen ways, most of them silent. “If I’m only a body,” he laughs, “I’m up shit creek.” His laugh is a gritty eruption of rock, salt, and breath. Like me, he writes poems, but he does it letter by letter on a propped keyboard, the mouth-stick wobbling between his teeth. That kind of pace keeps a poet accountable. He will never say, “The grass is very green,” when it is only green.
outputs.L2:
On the second floor, near the intersection of Hearst and Shattuck, he is permanently sealed inside an iron lung. When mealtime comes, he inches his head, slick with sweat, across what feels like an endless distance to the pillow’s edge. It takes time. With his sharp, bloodshot, pale-blue eyes, he directs me from the cabinet to the refrigerator: he wants his chicken burrito sliced into small mouthfuls, and a curved straw placed in his water glass, please.

How can a body spend its one life confined inside a cage? I watch him measure the gaps between the bars, then force himself through them by some ferocious inward pressure, a brief rage of escape that cannot hold. His determination is like a crowbar set at an angle, trying to lift the stubborn, immovable heaviness of the physical world. I observe him covertly, studying how he manages it. And he does manage it. Still, pain, in its complete solitude, has exactly the weight it has.

I come to him to examine the soul, asking the same question in a dozen forms, most of them unspoken. “If all I am is a body,” he says, laughing, “then I’m up shit creek.” His laughter breaks out rough and granular, made of stone, salt, and air. Like me, he writes poetry, but he composes it one letter at a time on a raised keyboard, a mouth-stick trembling between his teeth. A pace like that forces a poet to be exact. He would never write, “The grass is very green,” if it is merely green.
outputs.L3:
The man lives confined within an iron lung, a machine that sustains his breathing but severely limits his ability to move. His body is almost entirely immobilized, and even the simplest acts of communication require extraordinary effort. To express a need or a thought, he must rely on small, careful movements—gestures that demand patience from him and close attention from those around him. What might seem minor or automatic for others becomes, in his life, a deliberate and exhausting act.

The narrator watches this struggle with a sense of awe. The man’s condition is not presented simply as passive suffering, but as a constant battle against confinement. His body is restricted, yet his will remains active and forceful. Every attempt to communicate, every controlled movement, becomes an act of resistance against the limits imposed on him. The narrator sees in him a fierce determination to remain present, expressive, and fully human despite the machine and the paralysis that define so much of his daily existence.

The text also reflects deeply on the nature of pain. Pain is shown as something intensely private, difficult for others to measure or fully understand. Even when it is visible through the body’s struggle, its true weight belongs to the person who endures it. This leads to a broader meditation on the relationship between body and soul. The man’s body is trapped and dependent, but his inner life remains vivid, independent, and strong. The contrast between physical limitation and spiritual vitality becomes central to the narrator’s understanding of him.

Despite his condition, the man preserves humor, imagination, and creative energy. He is not reduced to his illness or his machine. He jokes, thinks, composes, and continues to make art. Using a mouth-stick, he writes poems one letter at a time, slowly building language through immense concentration and discipline. This process reveals not only his patience but also his refusal to let silence or immobility define him.

Because his writing is so slow and effortful, every word carries unusual weight. He cannot write carelessly or casually; each letter must be chosen and placed with intention. This gives his poetry a special precision. His poems are accountable to the labor that produces them. They emerge from time, pain, attention, and will, and for that reason they feel especially exact and deeply earned. Through his life and work, the man demonstrates that creativity can survive even extreme physical confinement, and that the human spirit can continue to speak with clarity and force under the most difficult conditions.
outputs.L4:
The passage presents a sustained, intimate portrait of a severely disabled poet whose life is confined within the narrow limits of an iron lung. Rather than treating him sentimentally or reducing him to his illness, it observes him with close, almost unsparing attention. The details of his daily existence become central: the difficulty of eating, the careful management of breath, the limited movements available to him, the strain of speech, and the slow, exacting labor of writing with a mouth-stick. Through these physical realities, the passage asks what it means to live, think, and create when the body has become both prison and instrument.

The poet’s condition is not softened or romanticized. His suffering is private, continuous, and deeply bodily. Every action that others might take for granted requires effort, discipline, and endurance. Eating is not merely eating; it is a procedure. Movement is not free motion; it is a negotiation with paralysis. Speech must be shaped against weakness and dependence. Writing, especially, becomes an act of extraordinary concentration. With the mouth-stick, each word is won slowly, letter by letter, through patience and precision. The process reveals the cost of art when the artist’s physical powers have been drastically reduced.

Yet the passage is not only about pain or confinement. It is also about will. The poet’s body may be restricted, but his mind remains intensely active and demanding. His persistence does not appear as simple cheerfulness or easy heroism. It is fiercer and more disciplined than that. He insists on accuracy, on saying what he means, on making language answer to truth. His physical limitations do not weaken his artistic seriousness; in some ways, they sharpen it. Because every gesture and every word requires such effort, nothing can be careless. The conditions of his life force a kind of severity, a hard clarity that becomes part of his poetic strength.

The passage also explores the relation between body and soul. The iron lung encloses the poet, sustaining him while also marking the extremity of his dependence. His body is vulnerable, painful, and nearly immobile, but the passage suggests that the soul is not identical with bodily freedom. Something inward remains unconfined: a force of attention, judgment, imagination, and desire. This inward life does not erase suffering, nor does it magically overcome disability. Instead, it exists within suffering and against it. The poet’s freedom is therefore not the freedom to move where he wishes, but the freedom to think, to make, to endure, and to speak with precision.

In this way, the passage transforms limitation into a source of insight. The poet’s confinement strips life down to its essentials: breath, pain, language, dependence, courage, and the need to create meaning. His art does not arise in spite of his condition alone, but also through the intense pressures that condition imposes. The difficulty of writing makes each poem a record of resistance. The restricted body becomes the site of a profound spiritual and artistic struggle.

Ultimately, the passage finds dignity in the poet’s persistence. It does not deny the harshness of his existence, but it refuses to see him only as an object of pity. His life in the iron lung is marked by suffering, but also by discipline, intelligence, and fierce creative purpose. Through his painstaking work, he achieves a hard-won freedom of spirit. The passage suggests that human dignity does not depend entirely on physical power or outward independence. Even under extreme constraint, the will to make truth in language can affirm the depth and resilience of the human soul.
outputs.L5: Two friends met on Hearst Avenue just as the afternoon light began to soften over Berkeley. They walked toward Shattuck, talking about old bookstores, busy cafés, and the quiet charm of the neighborhood. Hearst felt calm and reflective, while Shattuck was full of movement, voices, and the rhythm of the city. counterfactuals.prompt: Write a vivid first-person literary vignette about visiting a paralyzed poet in an iron lung near Hearst and Shattuck, focusing on embodiment, willpower, pain, and the precision of poetry.
counterfactuals.output:
Near Hearst and Shattuck, the traffic kept making its bright, indifferent argument: buses sighing at the curb, bicycles clicking past like small machines of thought, students lifting paper cups to their mouths as if drinking from the future. I climbed a narrow staircase above a storefront that smelled of ink, dust, and oranges, and at the end of the hall I found the room where the poet lived inside his iron lung.

It was larger than I expected, not a coffin but a vessel: a long blue cylinder with a polished rim around his neck, a machine with the patience of weather. It breathed him with a slow, authoritative rhythm. In. Out. In. Out. The whole room obeyed it. The curtains moved when it moved. The cup of water beside him trembled faintly. Even my own ribs, treacherous and free, seemed to adjust themselves to its command.

His head lay on a small white pillow, turned toward the window. He had black hair combed carefully back, a face sharpened by pain and attention, and eyes so alive they made the rest of the room appear unfinished. The machine enclosed all but him: the thinking portion, the suffering portion, the portion that could still choose. I had come expecting weakness, and instead felt I had entered the presence of an extreme discipline.

“Sit where I can see you,” he said.

His voice was soft, but it had edges. Each word had been purchased. Breath arrived to him mechanically, but speech was his rebellion against the machine’s timing. He waited for the negative pressure to fill him, then released a phrase, measured and exact. Not a syllable wasted. I understood, with a force that embarrassed me, how careless I had been with language all my life—spilling it, spending it, letting sentences loll and wander because my lungs could afford extravagance.

On the table beside him were pages held down by a stone. A pencil lay there too, useless to his hands, though not to him. He dictated poems to anyone patient enough to become his instrument. A comma took five minutes. A line break took longer. He would close his eyes, descend somewhere inward, and return with a correction so fine it seemed less like editing than surgery.

“Not ‘dark,’” he said once, after I read a draft aloud. “Say ‘unlit.’ Dark is too proud.”

I crossed it out.

The room was warm. The iron lung gave off a faint electrical smell, metallic and medicinal, like a hospital trying to dream itself into a workshop. Outside, a girl laughed on the sidewalk, and the sound rose cleanly through the open window. His eyes shifted toward it—not with envy, exactly, and not with resignation. Something more difficult lived there. Recognition, perhaps. The world had not stopped offering itself just because he could not go out into it. It came through windows, through visitors, through the pressure of air, through pain’s narrow gate.

He told me pain was not one thing. It had colors, climates, habits. There was the hot wire in the shoulder, the grinding stone in the hip, the swarm of needles under the skin where sensation was supposed to be absent. There was also the pain of being interpreted: saint, tragedy, lesson, miracle. He had no patience for any of it.

“I am not brave before breakfast,” he said. “Remember that.”

Then he smiled, and the smile altered everything—not because it softened him, but because it revealed the presence of will as something muscular, though no muscle obeyed him. His will did not stride or lift or grasp. It selected. It endured. It revised. It refused the false word. It made a life out of infinitesimals: a breath, a pause, a vowel, the exact weight of “unlit” instead of “dark.”

I watched his mouth shape a line. The machine inhaled for him; he waited. The machine exhaled; he spoke.

“Again,” he said.

So I read the stanza again.

“No,” he whispered. “The stress is wrong.”

Outside, the afternoon lowered itself over Berkeley. Light slid down the brick buildings. The intersection at Hearst and Shattuck flashed and halted, flashed and halted, directing bodies through space: walk, don’t walk, walk. I became unbearably aware of my legs crossed beneath the chair, of my hand around the pen, of the animal luxury of scratching my eyebrow. My body felt suddenly loud, almost vulgar in its freedoms. His body, hidden inside the lung, had become a kind of silence around which language had to be built with absolute care.

When I rose to leave, the machine was still breathing, tireless and impersonal. He looked past me to the page.

“Take the poem,” he said. “But don’t trust it yet.”

On the street again, the air entered me without effort. I hated, for a moment, the ease of it. Then I heard his line in my head, tightened by pain, governed by breath, and I understood that precision was not ornament to him. It was survival. Poetry was the place where nothing paralyzed remained still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short prose piece in the style of a memoiristic essay, describing someone feeding and observing a disabled writer who types poems with a mouth-stick.
counterfactuals.output:
At noon I carried the soup to his desk, where the page waited on the screen with the patience of a held breath. He had already maneuvered his chair into position, the mouth-stick angled beside him like a thin wand. I set the bowl on the tray and tucked the napkin beneath his chin, an intimacy that never became casual, though we performed it every day.

He accepted each spoonful with a concentration that made me ashamed of my own haste. Between bites his eyes went to the window, to the maple tree worried by wind, to the small congregation of sparrows at the feeder. He seemed to be listening for something beneath the ordinary clatter of the room: the radiator ticking, my chair creaking, the spoon touching porcelain.

When he was finished, I wiped his mouth and placed the stick carefully between his teeth. His whole body grew still except for the precise movement of his head. Letter by letter, he entered the poem. It was slow work, almost monastic, and yet nothing about it felt diminished. The words appeared with a severity I had never achieved in speech: branch, hunger, wing, mercy.

I used to think I was there to help him live. Over time I understood that I was also there to witness a discipline of attention. He took the world in by the spoonful and returned it, transformed, one keystroke at a time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical paragraph about a man confined to an iron lung who still writes poetry, seen through the eyes of another poet who comes to “study the soul.”
counterfactuals.output: I came to him with my notebook and my solemn hunger, saying I wished to study the soul, but the soul was already there, breathing in iron. He lay within the great dark cylinder like a seed sealed in winter, his face lifted free at one end, pale and luminous, the only open window in a house made of machinery. Around him the bellows sighed and labored, borrowing the work of his chest, yet his eyes moved with a wind no engine could supply. He spoke his poems slowly, as if each word had to travel from some deep country of fire through a narrow pass of pain: moon, mother, river, God, the blue bruise of evening, the stubborn grass. I had thought confinement meant silence, but he made of stillness a field; I had thought the body was the boundary, but he crossed it line by line. Watching him, I understood that poetry was not the luxury of the free, but the breath beneath breath—the hidden bird beating its wings against the ribs of the world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intense, image-rich scene set in Berkeley at Hearst and Shattuck, where the narrator helps a brilliant blue-eyed man in an iron lung eat a burrito and reflects on the body as a cage.
counterfactuals.output:
At Hearst and Shattuck, the buses breathed diesel into the evening like tired animals, and the whole intersection flashed and shuddered under green lights, red lights, the white sweep of headlights over wet asphalt. Berkeley smelled of eucalyptus, exhaust, coffee grounds, and rain lifting from the pavement. Students streamed past with backpacks hunched like shells, laughing into their phones, vanishing under awnings and neon signs. Above us, the hills were already dark.

He lay inside the iron lung as if inside a piece of weather.

It had been rolled up beside the curb near the bus stop, a long cylindrical machine the color of old hospital walls, its metal sides dull under the streetlamps. Hoses flexed and sighed. The bellows drew and released with a patient, mechanical insistence, a tide caged in steel. Each breath arrived for him from outside his body.

His head rested at one end, free and impossibly alive.

His eyes were brilliant blue—not pale, not sentimental, but electric, the blue of a gas flame or a sudden opening in storm clouds over the bay. They made the rest of the intersection seem underdeveloped, unfinished. The traffic lights, the lit windows, the blue-white glare of the pharmacy sign—all of it dimmed when he looked at me.

“You ever try eating a burrito lying down?” he asked.

His voice was dry and amused, edged with effort. The machine answered after him: hush, pull, hush, pull.

I held the foil-wrapped burrito in both hands like an offering. It was heavy and hot, seeping warmth through the aluminum, fragrant with carne asada, cilantro, onions, rice, beans, salsa roja—dense as a brick, tender as a secret. Steam escaped when I peeled the foil back, and for a moment the sharp green smell of lime cut through the street’s oil and rubber.

“Not successfully,” I said.

“Then we’re pioneers.”

People looked and then looked away. That was the choreography. Their eyes struck the iron cylinder, recoiled, found refuge in crosswalk signals, shop windows, the cracked sidewalk. A woman with a canvas tote slowed, her face softening with pity so visible it was almost violent, then hurried on as if ashamed of having been seen seeing.

He saw it all. His mouth twitched.

“Angle of approach is everything,” he said.

I knelt beside him on the cold concrete. Rainwater had gathered in the seams of the sidewalk, reflecting the traffic in broken strips of red and gold. The iron lung exhaled beside me, massive and intimate. Up close, it seemed less like a coffin than a stubborn instrument, a machine built to negotiate with death one breath at a time.

I folded the foil down carefully, tucking it so it wouldn’t scrape his chin. The tortilla glistened where salsa had soaked through. His lips parted. I brought the burrito toward him slowly, absurdly nervous, as though feeding him were surgery, sacrament, theft.

“Higher,” he said. “No, your other higher.”

I laughed, and he smiled with his eyes first.

When he bit down, it was with concentration so complete the intersection fell away. His jaw worked. A grain of rice clung to the corner of his mouth. I wiped it with a napkin before asking, and then felt a flash of embarrassment—mine, not his—at the intimacy of it. But he only watched me with those incandescent eyes.

“Good?” I asked.

He closed his eyes briefly.

“Cathedral good.”

The machine inhaled for him. The machine exhaled for him. Somewhere behind us, a man shouted at a bus driver. A bike chain clicked. A siren unfurled down University Avenue, thin and bright. The burrito steamed in my hand, shedding its heat into the dark.

Again, I lifted it. Again, he took a bite.

There was nothing delicate about his hunger. It was fierce, specific, intelligent. He wanted more salsa. He wanted the bite from the middle, not the end, because the end was “structurally compromised.” He wanted lime squeezed on the exposed rice. He wanted me not to hover like a nurse in a Victorian death scene.

“I’m not dying tonight,” he said. “I’m eating.”

So I fed him.

And while I did, I could not stop thinking about the body.

Not his body only—mine too. Everyone’s. The young men striding past in denim jackets, all shoulders and appetite. The woman at the crosswalk tugging a child back from the curb. The old man leaning on a cane outside the liquor store. The bodies in motion, bodies obeying, bodies failing quietly beneath coats and skin.

We pretend the body is a home because the alternative is unbearable. We hang pictures in it. We learn its hallways. We say my hand, my mouth, my heart, as if possession were the same as command. But the body is also a cage made of meat and timing. A cage with appetites painted on the bars. A cage that can rust, revolt, lock from the inside.

His cage was visible. Mine was not.

That was the difference, and it was smaller than I wanted it to be.

The iron lung gleamed under the streetlight, bolted and riveted, a second rib cage built by strangers. It surrounded him with its blunt fact of limitation, yet his gaze kept escaping it. His mind moved in the air above us, quick as a bird. He asked me what I was reading. He disagreed with my answer before I finished giving it. He quoted Spinoza between bites of burrito and accused Berkeley of having “too many bookstores and not enough mercy.” He laughed at his own joke, and the machine breathed him through it.

A drop of salsa slid down the tortilla onto the foil. I caught it with the napkin.

“You’re good at this,” he said.

“At burritos?”

“At not making it tragic.”

I looked at him then. Really looked. The blue eyes. The stubble along his jaw. The tiny scar near his temple. The vulnerable hollow of his throat where the collar of the machine sealed around him. His head floating at the mouth of the cylinder like a moon emerging from an eclipse.

“I don’t know how not to,” I admitted.

He was quiet. The traffic shifted. A bus knelt at the curb with a hydraulic sigh, its doors folding open, yellow light spilling out over the sidewalk.

Finally he said, “Tragedy is when nobody brings salsa.”

I laughed too hard, almost dropping the burrito, and he grinned with sudden boyish triumph.

The last bite was mostly tortilla, rice, and charred meat. I held it carefully. He chewed slowly, solemn now, as though honoring the end of something. When he swallowed, a small silence opened between us.

The iron lung pulled breath into him.

Released it.

Pulled.

Released.

Above Shattuck, fog moved low and silver between the buildings. The streetlights wore halos. The world looked briefly submerged, the city sunk under dark water, all of us moving along the bottom in our fragile suits of bone.

I balled up the foil. My fingers smelled of cumin, lime, and metal.

“Thank you,” he said.

But it did not feel like gratitude belonged only to him. I had fed him because his hands could not rise, because the machine held his chest in its iron rhythm, because the body had made its cruel little contract with him and he had found ways to outargue it. Yet kneeling there at Hearst and Shattuck, with rain on my knees and traffic burning past, I felt as if he had given me something larger and more terrible than thanks.

He had made the cage visible.

He had shown me that the self is not the body, though it suffers through it. Not the machine, though it may need one. Not the pity reflected in strangers’ eyes. Not even the hunger, though hunger proves we are still here.

The self was the blue flame looking out.

The self was the joke sharpened against despair.

The self was the man inside the iron lung, asking for extra salsa, refusing to become a symbol while the whole city tried to turn him into one.

The light changed. Cars surged forward. Somewhere, bells rang from the campus tower, blurred by fog.

The machine breathed.

He looked up at me, eyes bright enough to wound the dark, and said, “Next time, Thai.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary nonfiction passage about disability, pain, and artistic discipline, featuring a poet who can only type letter by letter with a mouth-stick and refuses imprecise language.
counterfactuals.output:
By nine in the morning, the poet had already corrected three verbs.

The room was small, arranged around the reach of his mouth-stick: the angled keyboard, the monitor lifted to eye height, the cup with a straw, the bell he disliked using, the window with its unhelpful square of sky. Everything had been measured, repositioned, and made obedient to a body that would not obey him. The body was not an emblem. It was not a lesson. It was where the pain lived.

He typed one letter at a time.

The stick, clamped between his teeth, moved with a precision that made anyone watching fall quiet. Not out of pity—he hated pity, which he called “a failure of imagination”—but because the labor was undeniable. The tip hovered, descended, struck. A letter appeared. Then another. A word gathered itself slowly, like a figure crossing a field in snow.

If the word was wrong, he deleted it.

Visitors sometimes begged him not to. They did not say beg; they said, “It’s close enough,” or “We know what you mean,” or “Don’t tire yourself.” At this, his eyes sharpened. Close enough was the language of elevators that stopped between floors, of doctors who rounded down suffering, of ramps built too steep for anyone to use with dignity. Close enough was a door labeled accessible and locked from the inside.

“No,” he would say, if he had the breath. If not, he would erase the word anyway.

Pain had made him economical, but not vague. He understood the difference. Economy was a discipline; vagueness was surrender. Pain narrowed the day into intervals—medication, spasm, exhaustion, brief weather systems of relief—but inside those intervals he insisted on exactness. A line could take an hour. A stanza might consume a week. He did not romanticize this. He was not grateful for the suffering that slowed his work. He considered pain a thief with bad taste, always stealing time and leaving behind clichés.

What astonished me was not that he wrote despite the pain, but that he refused to let pain become his editor.

He would not allow it to bully a sentence into sentimentality. He would not let it excuse a lazy metaphor. When a draft described his shoulder as “burning,” he paused, eyes fixed on the screen, then struck the backspace key seven times. Burning was too clean, too common, too much like a match. What he felt was serrated, electrical, deep—“a hooked brightness under the bone.” That stayed.

He believed words had moral weight. To name a thing poorly was not merely to fail aesthetically; it was to add fog to a world already dangerous with misunderstanding. Disability, he said, was not a symbol for brokenness, nor a shortcut to wisdom, nor a costume for courage. It was a condition of living in a body among buildings, systems, weather, strangers, stairs. Pain was not purity. Dependence was not defeat. Help was not humiliation. He had spent years cutting false grandeur from his poems the way one cuts rot from fruit.

And yet the poems were not sterile. They were full of appetite: black coffee, lilacs after rain, a woman’s laugh in a hallway, the blue flame of a gas stove, the particular silence after snow begins. His discipline did not make the work bloodless. It made the blood visible.

In the afternoon, fatigue loosened his grip. The mouth-stick slipped once, clattered against the tray, and he closed his eyes. No one moved. We had learned that assistance, too, required grammar: the right action, the right timing, the consent implied or withheld by a glance. After a moment he opened his eyes and looked toward the stick. His aide placed it back between his teeth.

He returned to the line.

On the screen were five words:

*Mercy is not the same—*

He stared at them for a long time. The room hummed around him: computer, heater, the faint traffic below. His jaw trembled. The cursor pulsed, indifferent and patient.

Then he typed, letter by letter:

*—as being spared.*

He read the completed line once, then again. Nothing in his face softened, exactly. Satisfaction, for him, was not dramatic. It was the absence of objection. It was the rare stillness that came when no word had betrayed the thing it was asked to carry.

Outside, the sky went on being careless and bright. Inside, he began the next line.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
